The obvious tool is a ruler. Straight-line distance. But a ruler also counts how long each vector is. And in an embedding, length mostly tracks how common a word is, not what it means. So we measure the angle instead. That's cosine similarity. These two point the same way, and one's five times longer. The ruler says five point seven apart. Cosine says one. A perfect match. At a right angle, cosine is zero. Unrelated. Pointing opposite ways, it's minus one.

That's enough for a working search. Five tiny documents, each scored on four themes. Now ask, how did the company perform financially? Top hit, earnings beat analyst expectations, at point nine nine eight. Not one word in common with the question. The search runs on meaning, not on text.

It does have blind spots. The drug is effective, and the drug is not effective, land almost on top of each other. Close isn't true, and it isn't always useful. So real systems add a second pass that actually reads the top hits. And one vector per word has a bigger problem. Some words mean nothing until you see their neighbours.

The trophy didn't fit in the suitcase because it was too big. What was too big? The trophy. Make it too small, and now it's the suitcase. The pronoun never changed. Its meaning comes from the words around it. Attention is how each token pulls in information from the others, weighted by how relevant each one is.

To do that, every token makes three vectors. A query: what am I looking for? A key: what do I offer? And a value: what I hand over when I'm picked. The pronoun's query is compared with every key, for one score each. Softmax turns the scores into weights that add up to one. In the lesson's example, the pronoun puts point seven two of its attention on trophy.
